So they need to have these phones unlocked in a way that doesn't show that the phone is compromised already and with a search warrant. So yes in some small way they need Apples help.

This is one part of the situation that lends the most credence to the idea that this is all smoke and mirrors, just a tactic to make people think they can't get into iPhones but they truly already can.

No they don't. They could absolutely rip the phone and clone it on to a super computer cluster and have it cracked in less time than this court case is going to take.

Additionally, it is extremely unlikely that they need anything off that phone in the first place. He destroyed most of the incriminating evidence before the attack, including both his and his wife's personal cell phones. The phone they are trying to crack is his government issued work phone.

While I'm completely on Apple's side in this matter, the article makes it sound like the decap and FIB (Focused Ion Beam) work is easy and foolproof and the FBI should have no problem with a physical attack. I don't agree. First, you have to remove the chip from the board and process off enough packaging to expose the die. Then you need to etch off the glass protecting the die. At this point, your clock is ticking. The now-exposed circuit will degrade unless kept in a fab-like environment, which is expensive and prone mishap because all this is a human operation. So, let's assume you've decapped the part and conditioned it properly for ion beam work without damaging it, which is no small task. Next, consider the "fuses" that are being talked about are almost certainly flash cells. These cells are almost certainly covered by metal to prevent easy probing. Removing this metal will almost certainly cause enough local charging to perturb the state of the flash cells. In fact , the entire memory array is at risk for bits here and there getting flipped from this kind of work. In other words, the FIB work suggested is very likely to fail. It's not that it can't be done. It's just that's it's very challenging to do, and you only get 1 shot. Screw anything up and the part is dead, or at compromised to the point of not being very useful.

I know this sounds fishy, buy I can speak from personal design experience the chips I worked on (8 & 16bit microcontrollers) had no backdoor in our code protection. If the customer wanted us to unlock something. Oh well. If we wanted to unlock a part for RMA purposes, oh well. We even went so far as to "program" some aspects of ROM devices in the diffusion layer so no manner of visual inspection could be used, nor could a simple metal cut be made to defeat the lock. Code protection is super important in that market, and no one, and I mean no one, took it more seriously than we did. I applaud Apple for doing the same. At the same time, I have to acknowledge if Apple did their job right, the FBI (or the NSA or whoever) is not going to find it easy to physically hack their way in.

Sadly most people don't have any idea on how IT security works, especially when it's integrated at the firmware or hardware level. Most don't even know the difference of when Apple did single point data retrieval and what the FBI is currently asking for with an encryption back door.
Sure they can, but if they do and the information is presented to court as evidence, a smart lawyer would have it thrown out on the basis of violating the 4th amendment.
